Notes: Year Established basis: Josephus (Against Apion 2.4) claims Jewish settlement from the city's foundation: 'it was Alexander himself that gave them that place for their habitation', with privileges equal to the Macedonians, in a quarter near the sea. Josephus' claim is apologetic; Encyclopaedia Judaica (Tcherikover) dates the settlement to the early 3rd c. BCE. Founding year 332/331 BCE.

c.; Josephus (Antiquities 12.1.1): Ptolemy I son of Lagus seized Jerusalem, took 'a great many captives' to Egypt, distributed many into garrisons and 'at Alexandria gave them equal privileges of citizens with the Macedonians'. Ptolemy I's capture of Jerusalem is variously dated 320/312/302 BCE; Josephus gives no year. No number of settlers in Alexandria given.

c. (early Ptolemaic, approx.); Jewish Encyclopedia (E. Schürer): history of the Jews of Alexandria 'dates from the foundation of the city by Alexander the Great, 332 B.C.'; 'A separate section of the city was assigned to them by the first Ptolemies'; Jews formed 'a very large portion of the population under the successors of Alexander'. Its statement that Ptolemy I distributed 30,000 Jewish soldiers as garrisons 'over the land' is a regional/military figure for Egypt, not Alexandria's population.

c.; Encyclopaedia Judaica (V. Tcherikover, via Jewish Virtual Library): 'Jews settled in Alexandria at the beginning of the third century B.C.E.' (scholarly dating of the settlement; Josephus places them there already under Alexander). Beginning of 3rd c. BCE taken as c. 290.

Philo, Life of Moses 2.25-44: Greek translation of the Jewish law (Septuagint) under Ptolemy II Philadelphus on the island of Pharos in front of Alexandria; Philo (1st c. CE) adds that 'every year a solemn assembly' and festival is held on Pharos attended by Jews and others. Reign of Ptolemy II 283-246 BCE, midpoint used; the story contains legendary elements but attests an Alexandrian Greek-speaking Jewish community in the 3rd c. BCE.

c.; Josephus (Against Apion 2.5): under Ptolemy VI Philometor and Cleopatra II the kingdom's army was commanded by 'Onias and Dositheus, both Jews', cited by Josephus in defence of the Alexandrian Jews' loyalty. Reign 180-145 BCE, midpoint used. Attests Jewish standing at the Ptolemaic court; no count.

c.; Jewish Encyclopedia (Gottheil & Wendland): Aristobulus, an 'Alexandrian Peripatetic philosopher', Jewish author whose more reliable dating makes him 'a contemporary of Ptolemy Philometor (middle of second century B.C.)' (cf. 2 Macc 1:10). Named Jewish individual in Alexandria.

2nd c. BCE (midpoint); synagogue dedication inscription from Alexandria (IEgJud/JIGRE 9 = CIJ II 1433), grey marble plaque now in the Graeco-Roman Museum: 'the Judeans dedicated the sacred enclosure, the prayer-house (proseuchē), and its accoutrements' to the Most High God. Organized community with a prayer house.

c.; Strabo quoted by Josephus (Antiquities 14.7.2): the Jews have a place 'peculiarly allotted to this nation at Alexandria, which is a large part of that city', and 'an ethnarch allowed them, who governs the nation, and distributes justice to them'. Strabo's passage is set in the context of Mithridates/Sulla (c. 88-85 BCE); date approximate. Large organized community, no count.

c.; Josephus (Against Apion 2.4): a pillar at Alexandria 'contains the privileges which the great [Julius] Caesar bestowed upon the Jews' (Caesar in Alexandria 48-47 BCE). Confirmation of communal rights; no count.

Proseuchē dedication inscription, Alexandria (IEgJud/JIGRE 13; = CIJ II 1432, the Gabbari synagogue under Cleopatra VII): 'Alypos constructed this prayer house (proseuchē) and dedicated it to the great god who listens. Year 15' = 37 BCE. Second documented prayer house in the city.

Papyrus BGU 4,1151 (Alexandrian notarial archive, Abusir el-Meleq cartonnage), dated 27/25 April 13 BCE: a legacy of Theodoros validated 'through the archive of the Jews' (archeion ton Ioudaion), interpreted (Fraser; Tcherikover-Fuks) as the Alexandrian Jewish community's own notarial office, functioning from Ptolemaic times into early Roman rule (P. Druille 2021). Organized community with its own public record office.

Augustan period (27 BCE-14 CE, midpoint); Jewish Encyclopedia (Schürer): under Augustus a gerusia replaced the ethnarch at the head of the Alexandrian Jews; it 'numbered, as in Jerusalem, seventy-one members', presided over by archons. Synagogues 'distributed all over the city' per Philo. Council members are a subset, not a population.

Around the turn of the era (year 1 used); Posen Library guide (Carol Bakhos): Alexandria's population 'may have been 30–40 percent Jewish'. Percentage only; no absolute number of Jews given, so Population left blank.

Early Roman period (midpoint 4 CE); Andrew Harker (Loyalty and Dissidence in Roman Egypt, CUP 2008, Appendix II 'The status of the Alexandrian Jews', chapter summary): the Jewish community was 'around a fifth to a third of the population according to modern estimates'. Proportion only; Population blank.

Roman era (early Roman midpoint 4 CE); Wikipedia (last resort, citing T. Donaldson 2000 and M. Redies, Brill's New Pauly): Jews comprised 'about 35% of the city's population during the Roman era'. Proportion only; Population blank.

Philo, In Flaccum: the city 'has five districts', of which 'two are called the quarters of the Jews' (§55) because most Jews lived there; in the pogrom of 38 CE under prefect Flaccus the Jews were 'crammed... into a very small portion of one' quarter, synagogues destroyed (§53), 38 members of the council of elders scourged (§74-75), Jews 'stripped of above four hundred dwellings' (§94). Philo's figure of 'not less than a million' (§43) covers the Jews of Alexandria and the whole country to Ethiopia (regional, ancient figure, generally considered exaggerated) and is not used as Population.

Sandra Gambetti, The Alexandrian Riots of 38 C.E. (2009), reviewed by T. Seland (BMCR 2010.12.63): in summer 38 'the Alexandrian Jews were pushed back into the Δ section of the city'; 'many Jews were living outside the Δ district'; tensions grew 'not least due to their increasing numbers'. Scholarly interpretation; no count.

Gregory E. Sterling (Marginalia Review): Philo, his brother Alexander and nephew Tiberius Julius Alexander were members of the Jewish embassy from Alexandria to Gaius Caligula after the pogrom; 'the size of the Jewish community within it exceeded the entire population of Jerusalem'. Embassy c. 39/40 CE. Comparative statement only; no number.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library): after the 38 CE riots in which 'Many Jews were murdered' and 'all the Jews were confined to one-quarter of the city', on Caligula's death (41 CE) the Jews armed themselves and, with support from Jews of Egypt and the Land of Israel, fell upon the Greeks; suppressed by Rome; Claudius restored their religious rights. Also mentions Nicanor 'the Alexandrian' who donated the Temple gates (ossuary near Jerusalem).

Letter of Claudius to the Alexandrians (P.Lond. 6.1912), 41 CE (published 10 Nov. 41): refers to 'the riots and feud (or rather, if the truth be told, the war) with the Jews'; Jews to enjoy their privileges 'in a city not their own', 'not to bring in or admit Jews who come down the river from Egypt or from Syria'.

Modern scholarly estimate (J. Mélèze Modrzejewski, The Jews of Egypt, as summarized by COJS): taking Josephus' 7.5 million for Roman Egypt (c. 8 million total), 'The Jews could have represented about 4 percent of the total, somewhat more than 300,000 persons', 'over half of whom lived in Alexandria'. Population = derived lower bound (over half of c. 300,000 = more than 150,000). Roman period, 1st c. CE midpoint used. [Review fix: Population 150000 moved to Notes; the 150,000 is the agent's own arithmetic ("over half" of "more than 300,000" Jews of Egypt), not a figure stated by the source]
c.; Acts 18:24: 'a Jew named Apollos from Alexandria', 'well-versed in the scriptures', came to Ephesus (c. 52 CE, during Paul's mission). Named Alexandrian Jew.

Josephus, Jewish War 2.487-498: Jews lived together in 'that part of the city that was called Delta'; in 66 CE prefect Tiberius Julius Alexander sent troops into Delta 'until... 50,000 Jews lay dead'. Death toll (ancient figure), not a population count; Population blank.

Modrzejewski (The Jews of Egypt, pp. 186-189, via COJS) on the 66 CE massacre: 'the number of dead was most probably less than fifty thousand, the figure put forth by Josephus', but the events were 'a terrible trial for the Jews of Alexandria... as bad as the pogrom of 38 C.E., if not worse'. Community survived; no count.

Josephus, Jewish War 7.10.1: after the fall of Masada, Sicarii fled to Alexandria; 'the principal men of the senate' of the Alexandrian Jews 'got all the Jews together to an assembly' and handed them over; 'six hundred of them were caught immediately'. The 600 are refugee Sicarii, not residents; attests a functioning community and gerousia in 73/74 CE.
